{{Short description|Property of geometry, also used to generalize the notion of "distance" in metric spaces}}
{{No newcomer task|reason="Generalized polygon inequality" should not be linked to [[Generalized polygon]]}}
{{about||other inequalities associated with triangles|List of triangle inequalities}}

[[File:TriangleInequality.svg|thumb|Three examples of the triangle inequality for triangles with sides of lengths {{mvar|x}}, {{mvar|y}}, {{mvar|z}}. The top example shows a case where {{mvar|z}} is much less than the sum {{math|''x'' + ''y''}} of the other two sides,  and the bottom example shows a case where the side {{mvar|z}} is only slightly less than {{math|''x'' + ''y''}}.]]

In [[mathematics]], the '''triangle inequality''' states that for any [[triangle]] in [[Euclidean space]], the sum of the [[length]]s of any two sides must be greater than or equal to the length of the third side.<ref name=Khamsi>{{cite book |title=An introduction to metric spaces and fixed point theory |author1=Mohamed A. Khamsi |author2=William A. Kirk |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4qXbEpAK5eUC&pg=PA8 |chapter=§1.4 The triangle inequality in {{math|'''R'''<sup>n</sup>}} |isbn=0-471-41825-0 |year=2001 |publisher=Wiley-IEEE}}</ref> If {{mvar|a}}, {{mvar|b}}, and {{mvar|c}} are the lengths of the sides of a triangle then:
<math display=block>c \leq a + b.</math>
The same [[Inequality (mathematics)|inequality]] holds when the sides of the triangle are relabeled, so also {{tmath|b \leq a + c}} and {{tmath|a \leq b + c}}. When one side length is equal to the sum of the other two, {{tmath|1= c = a + b}}, the triangle is [[degenerate triangle|degenerate]], with zero area.

The triangle inequality implies a related statement for [[Euclidean vector]]s, also called the ''triangle inequality''; if {{math|'''u'''}} and {{math|'''v'''}} are vectors (directed magnitudes, usually drawn as arrows), then {{math|'''u'''}}, {{math|'''v'''}}, and their sum {{math|'''u''' + '''v'''}} can be pictured as sides that are assembled into a triangle, with each vector's [[Norm (mathematics)|norm]] as the length of the corresponding side. Therefore
<math display=block>\|\mathbf u + \mathbf v\| \leq \|\mathbf u\| + \|\mathbf v\|.</math>

The triangle inequality also holds in some contexts other than Euclidean space. For example, it holds for [[spherical triangle|triangles on a sphere]] and [[Hyperbolic triangle|in the hyperbolic plane]]. But it does not hold in some contexts, for example [[Minkowski spacetime]].

The triangle inequality is one of the defining properties of a distance function in a [[metric space]]; if {{mvar|X}}, {{mvar|Y}}, and {{mvar|Z}} are any three points, only a function {{mvar|d}} which satisfies the triangle inequality,
<math display=block>d(X, Z) \leq d(X, Y) + d(Y, Z),</math>
is considered to be a proper notion of distance. The analog of the triangle inequality for vectors is also a defining property of the norm in [[normed vector space]]s.

==Euclidean geometry==

[[File:Euclid triangle inequality.svg|thumb|Euclid's construction for proof of the triangle inequality for plane geometry.]]

The triangle inequality theorem appears in [[Euclid's Elements|Euclid's ''Elements'']] as proposition 20 of Book I:

{{bi|left=1.6|''In any triangle the sum of any two sides is greater than the remaining one.''<ref name=Joyce/>}}

Euclid proved it using the construction shown in the figure.<ref name=Jacobs>{{cite book |page=201 |author=Harold R. Jacobs |title=Geometry: seeing, doing, understanding |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=XhQRgZRDDq0C&pg=PA201 |isbn=0-7167-4361-2 |edition=3rd |publisher=Macmillan |year=2003}}
</ref> Beginning with triangle {{mvar|ABC}}, the side {{math|{{overline|''AB''}}}} is extended by the same length as {{mvar|{{overline|BC}}}} to a new point {{mvar|D}}, forming an [[isosceles triangle]] {{mvar|CBD}}, which has two equal angles {{mvar|BDC}} and {{mvar|BCD}}, labeled {{tmath|\alpha}}. Angle {{mvar|ACD}}, labeled {{tmath|\beta}}, contains angle {{mvar|BCD}}, so {{tmath|\beta > \alpha}}. Therefore side {{math|{{overline|''AD''}}}} must be longer than side {{math|{{overline|''AC''}}}} (by proposition I.19). However: 
<math display="block">\overline{AD} = \overline{AB} + \overline{BD} = \overline{AB} + \overline{BC},</math> 
so the sum of the lengths of sides {{mvar|{{overline|AB}}}} and {{mvar|{{overline|BC}}}} is larger than the length of {{mvar|{{overline|AC}}}}.<ref name=Joyce>
{{cite web
| url         = https://mathcs.clarku.edu/~djoyce/java/elements/bookI/propI20.html
| title       = Euclid's Elements, Book I, Proposition 20
| author      = David E. Joyce | author-link = David E. Joyce (mathematician)
| year        = 1997
| work        = Euclid's Elements
| publisher   = Dept. Math and Computer Science, Clark University
| access-date  = 2010-06-25
}}
</ref>

===Mathematical expression of the constraint on the sides of a triangle===

For a non-degenerate triangle with side lengths {{math|''a'', ''b'', ''c''}}, the triangle inequality states that
<math display="block">a + b > c,\quad b + c > a,\quad c + a > b.</math>
This set of three inequalities can be succinctly summarized as
<math display="block">|a - b| < c < a + b .</math>
Or, equivalently, as
<math display="block">\max(a, b, c) < \tfrac12(a + b + c)</math>
where {{math|max(''a'', ''b'', ''c'')}} is the length of the longest side. That is, the longest side of a triangle is always shorter than the [[semiperimeter]], {{tmath|1=s = \tfrac12(a+b+c)}}.

Another equivalent statement is that the area of a triangle with sides {{math|''a'', ''b'', ''c''}} and semiperimeter {{mvar|s}} must be a real number greater than zero. [[Heron's formula]] for the area is
<math display="block">
\begin{align}
\text{area} & = \sqrt{s(s-a)(s-b)(s-c)}  \\[3pt]
4\cdot \text{area} & =  \sqrt{(a+b+c)(-a+b+c)(a-b+c)(a+b-c)} \,.
\end{align}
</math>
In terms of either area expression, the triangle inequality imposed on all sides is equivalent to the condition that the expression under the square root sign be real and greater than zero (so that the area expression is real and greater than zero).

The triangle inequality provides upper bounds for ratios of side lengths; with sides labeled in ascending length order {{math|0 < ''a'' ≤ ''b'' ≤ ''c''}}:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
1&<\frac{c+a}{b}<3, \\
1&\le\min\left(\frac{c}{b}, \frac{b}{a}\right)<\varphi,
\end{align}</math>
where <math>\varphi = \tfrac12\bigl(1 + \sqrt5\bigr)</math> is the [[golden ratio]].<ref>''[[American Mathematical Monthly]]'', pp. 49-50, 1954.</ref>

===Right triangle===

[[File:Isosceles triangle made of right triangles.svg|thumb|Isosceles triangle with equal sides {{math|{{overline|AB}} {{=}} {{overline|AC}}}} divided into two right triangles by an altitude drawn from one of the two base angles.]]

In the case of right triangles, the triangle inequality specializes to the statement that the [[hypotenuse]] is greater than either of the two sides and less than their sum.<ref name=Palmer>
{{cite book |title=Practical mathematics for home study: being the essentials of arithmetic, geometry, algebra and trigonometry |author=Claude Irwin Palmer |url=https://archive.org/details/practicalmathema00palmiala |page=[https://archive.org/details/practicalmathema00palmiala/page/422 422] |publisher=McGraw-Hill |year=1919}}
</ref>

The second part of this theorem is already established above for any side of any triangle. The first part is established using the lower figure. In the figure, consider the right triangle {{mvar|ADC}}. An isosceles triangle {{mvar|ABC}} is constructed with equal sides {{math|''{{overline|AB}}'' {{=}} ''{{overline|AC}}''}}. From the [[triangle postulate]], the angles in the right triangle {{math|ADC}} satisfy:
<math display="block">\alpha + \gamma = \pi /2 \ .</math>
Likewise, in the isosceles triangle {{mvar|ABC}}, the angles satisfy:
<math display="block">2\beta + \gamma = \pi \ .</math>
Therefore,
<math display="block">\alpha = \pi/2 - \gamma ,\ \mathrm{while} \ \beta= \pi/2 - \gamma /2  \ ,</math>
and so, in particular,
<math display="block">\alpha < \beta \ .</math>
That means side {{mvar|AD}}, which is opposite to angle {{mvar|α}}, is shorter than side {{mvar|AB}}, which is opposite to the larger angle {{mvar|β}}. But {{math|''{{overline|AB}}'' {{=}} ''{{overline|AC}}''}}. Hence:
<math display="block">\overline{AC} > \overline{AD} \ .</math>
A similar construction shows {{math|''{{overline|AC}}'' > ''{{overline|DC}}''}}, establishing the theorem.

An alternative proof (also based upon the triangle postulate) proceeds by considering three positions for point {{mvar|B}}:<ref name=Zawaira>
{{cite book |title=A primer for mathematics competitions |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=A21T73sqZ3AC&pg=PA30 |chapter=Lemma 1: In a right-angled triangle the hypotenuse is greater than either of the other two sides |author1=Alexander Zawaira |author2=Gavin Hitchcock |isbn=978-0-19-953988-8 |year=2009 |publisher=Oxford University Press}}
</ref> (i) as depicted (which is to be proved), or (ii) {{mvar|B}} coincident with {{mvar|D}} (which would mean the isosceles triangle had two right angles as base angles plus the vertex angle {{mvar|γ}}, which would violate the [[triangle postulate]]), or lastly, (iii) {{mvar|B}} interior to the right triangle between points {{mvar|A}} and {{mvar|D}} (in which case angle {{mvar|ABC}} is an exterior angle of a right triangle {{mvar|BDC}} and therefore larger than {{math|''π''/2}}, meaning the other base angle of the isosceles triangle also is greater than {{math|''π''/2}} and their sum exceeds {{mvar|π}} in violation of the triangle postulate).

This theorem establishing inequalities is sharpened by [[Pythagoras' theorem]] to the equality that the square of the length of the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides.

===Generalization to any polygon===
The triangle inequality can be extended by [[mathematical induction]] to arbitrary [[polygonal path]]s. This gives the ''generalized polygon inequality'', which asserts that the total length of such a path is no less than the length of the straight line between its endpoints. Consequently, the length of any polygon side is always less than the sum of the other polygon side lengths.

====Relationship with shortest paths====
[[File:Arclength.svg|thumb|The arc length of a curve is defined as the least upper bound of the lengths of polygonal approximations.]]
This generalization can be used to prove that the shortest curve between two points in Euclidean geometry is a straight line.

No polygonal path between two points is shorter than the line between them. This implies that no curve can have an [[arc length]] less than the distance between its endpoints. By definition, the arc length of a curve is the [[least upper bound]] of the lengths of all polygonal approximations of the curve. The result for polygonal paths shows that the straight line between the endpoints is the shortest of all the polygonal approximations. Because the arc length of the curve is greater than or equal to the length of every polygonal approximation, the curve itself cannot be shorter than the straight line path.<ref>{{cite book|title=Numbers and Geometry|author=John Stillwell|author-link=John Stillwell|year=1997|publisher=Springer|isbn=978-0-387-98289-2|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=4elkHwVS0eUC&pg=PA95}} p. 95.</ref>

===Converse===

The converse of the triangle inequality theorem is also true: if three real numbers are such that each is less than the sum of the others, then there exists a triangle with these numbers as its side lengths and with positive area; and if one number equals the sum of the other two, there exists a degenerate triangle (that is, with zero area) with these numbers as its side lengths.

In either case, if the side lengths are {{mvar|a}}, {{mvar|b}}, {{mvar|c}} we can attempt to place a triangle in the [[Euclidean plane]] as shown in the diagram. We need to prove that there exists a real number {{mvar|h}} consistent with the values {{mvar|a}}, {{mvar|b}}, and {{mvar|c}}, in which case this triangle exists.

[[Image:Triangle with notations 3.svg|thumb|Triangle with altitude {{mvar|h}} cutting base {{mvar|c}} into {{math|''d'' + (''c'' − ''d'')}}.]]

By the [[Pythagorean theorem]] we have {{math|''b''{{sup|2}} {{=}} ''h''{{sup|2}} + ''d''{{sup|2}}}} and {{math|''a''{{sup|2}} {{=}} ''h''{{sup|2}} + (''c'' − ''d''){{sup|2}}}} according to the figure at the right. Subtracting these yields {{math|''a''{{sup|2}} − ''b''{{sup|2}} {{=}} ''c''{{sup|2}} − 2''cd''}}. This equation allows us to express {{mvar|d}} in terms of the sides of the triangle:
<math display="block">d=\frac{-a^2+b^2+c^2}{2c}.</math>
For the height of the triangle we have that {{math|''h''{{sup|2}} {{=}} ''b''{{sup|2}} − ''d''{{sup|2}}}}. By replacing {{mvar|d}} with the formula given above, we have

<math display="block">h^2 = b^2-\left(\frac{-a^2+b^2+c^2}{2c}\right)^2.</math>

For a real number {{mvar|h}} to satisfy this, {{math|''h''{{sup|2}}}} must be non-negative:
<math display="block">\begin{align}
  0 &\le b^2-\left(\frac{-a^2+b^2+c^2}{2c}\right)^2 \\[4pt]
  0 &\le \left(b- \frac{-a^2+b^2+c^2}{2c}\right) \left(b + \frac{-a^2+b^2+c^2}{2c}\right) \\[4pt]
  0 &\le \left(a^2-(b-c)^2)((b+c)^2-a^2 \right) \\[6pt]
  0 &\le (a+b-c)(a-b+c)(b+c+a)(b+c-a) \\[6pt]
  0 &\le (a+b-c)(a+c-b)(b+c-a)
\end{align}</math>
which holds if the triangle inequality is satisfied for all sides. Therefore, there does exist a real number <math>h</math> consistent with the sides <math>a, b, c</math>, and the triangle exists. If each triangle inequality holds [[strict inequality|strictly]], <math>h > 0</math> and the triangle is non-degenerate (has positive area); but if one of the inequalities holds with equality, so <math>h = 0</math>, the triangle is degenerate.

===Generalization to higher dimensions===
{{see also|Distance geometry#Cayley–Menger determinants}}

The area of a triangular face of a [[tetrahedron]] is less than or equal to the sum of the areas of the other three triangular faces.  More generally, in Euclidean space the hypervolume of an {{math|(''n'' − 1)}}-[[Facet (mathematics)|facet]] of an {{mvar|n}}-[[simplex]] is less than or equal to the sum of the hypervolumes of the other {{mvar|n}} facets.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Izumi |first=Shuzo |date=2016 |title=Sufficiency of simplex inequalities |url=https://www.ams.org/proc/2016-144-03/S0002-9939-2015-12756-6/ |journal=Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society |language=en |volume=144 |issue=3 |pages=1299–1307 |doi=10.1090/proc12756 |issn=0002-9939}}</ref>

Much as the triangle inequality generalizes to a polygon inequality, the inequality for a simplex of any dimension generalizes to a [[polytope]] of any dimension: the hypervolume of any facet of a polytope is less than or equal to the sum of the hypervolumes of the remaining facets.

In some cases the tetrahedral inequality is stronger than several applications of the triangle inequality.  For example, the triangle inequality appears to allow the possibility of four points {{mvar|A}}, {{mvar|B}}, {{mvar|C}}, and {{mvar|Z}} in Euclidean space such that distances
:{{math|1=''AB'' = ''BC'' = ''CA'' = 26}}
and
:{{math|1=''AZ'' = ''BZ'' = ''CZ'' = 14}}.
However, points with such distances cannot exist: the area of the {{math|26–26–26}} equilateral triangle {{math|''ABC''}} is <math display=inline>169\sqrt 3</math>, which is larger than three times <math display=inline>39\sqrt 3</math>, the area of a {{math|26–14–14}} isosceles triangle (all by [[Heron's formula]]), and so the arrangement is forbidden by the tetrahedral inequality.

==Spherical geometry==
In [[spherical geometry]], a triangle is formed from three points and three [[great circle]] arcs, each connecting a pair of the points.  There are two great circle arcs that connect a pair of points; except when the vertices are exactly opposite on the sphere, one of those arcs will be the short way around the sphere and the other will be the long way around the sphere.  In this geometry, the triangle inequality tells us that the smaller length of the two arcs connecting a pair of points will have length less than or equal to the sum of the lengths of the arcs connecting the other pairs of points.<ref name= Ramos>
{{cite book |title=Robotics: Science and Systems IV |author1=Oliver Brock |author2=Jeff Trinkle |author3=Fabio Ramos |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=fvCaQfBQ7qEC&pg=PA195 |page=195 |isbn=978-0-262-51309-8 |publisher=MIT Press |year=2009}}
</ref><ref name=Ramsay>
{{cite book |title=Introduction to hyperbolic geometry |author1=Arlan Ramsay |author2=Robert D. Richtmyer |url=https://archive.org/details/introductiontohy0000rams |url-access=registration |page=[https://archive.org/details/introductiontohy0000rams/page/17 17] |isbn=0-387-94339-0 |year=1995 |publisher=Springer}}
</ref>
That is, the triangle inequality gives {{math|1=''c'' ≤ ''a'' + ''b''}} whenever {{mvar|c}} is not more than 180° ({{mvar|π}}&nbsp;radians).  This can be written as {{math|1=sin(''c''/2) ≤ sin(''a''/2) + sin(''b''/2)}}, without having to check whether {{mvar|c}} exceeds 180°.

===Triangle inequality for cosine similarity===
{{further|Cosine similarity}}
By applying the cosine function to the triangle inequality and reverse triangle inequality for arc lengths and employing the angle addition and subtraction formulas for cosines, it follows immediately that<ref>{{cite conference |last=Schubert |first=Erich |title=A Triangle Inequality for Cosine Similarity |conference=International Conference on Similarity Search and Applications |date=2021 |location=Dortmund |doi=10.1007/978-3-030-89657-7_3 |publisher=Springer |arxiv=2107.04071 }}</ref>

<math display="block">\cos(u,w) \geq \cos(u,v) \cdot \cos(v,w) - \sqrt{\left(1-\cos(u,v)^2\right)\cdot\left(1-\cos(v,w)^2\right)}</math>

and

<math display="block">\cos(u,w) \leq \cos(u,v) \cdot \cos(v,w) + \sqrt{\left(1-\cos(u,v)^2\right)\cdot\left(1-\cos(v,w)^2\right)}\,.</math>

With these formulas, one needs to compute a [[square root]] for each triple of vectors {{math|{''u'', ''v'', ''w''}<nowiki/>}} that is examined rather than {{math|arccos(cos(''u'',''v''))}} for each pair of vectors {{math|{''u'', ''v''}<nowiki/>}} examined, and could be a performance improvement when the number of triples examined is less than the number of pairs examined.

==Normed vector space==
[[File:Vector-triangle-inequality.svg|thumb|Triangle inequality for norms of vectors.]]

In a [[normed vector space]] {{mvar|V}}, one of the defining properties of the [[norm (mathematics)|norm]] is the triangle inequality:

<math display=block>\|\mathbf u + \mathbf v\| \leq \|\mathbf u\| + \|\mathbf v\| \quad \forall \, \mathbf u, \mathbf v \in V</math>

That is, the norm of the [[Vector sum#Addition and subtraction|sum of two vectors]] is at most as large as the sum of the norms of the two vectors.  This is also referred to as [[subadditivity]]. For any proposed function to behave as a norm, it must satisfy this requirement.<ref name=Kress>
{{cite book |title=Numerical analysis |author=Rainer Kress |chapter=§3.1: Normed spaces |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=e7ZmHRIxum0C&pg=PA26 |page=26 |isbn=0-387-98408-9 |year=1988 |publisher=Springer}}</ref>

=== Triangle equality ===
If the normed space is [[euclidean space|Euclidean]], or, more generally, [[strictly convex space|strictly convex]], then the ''triangle equality''<math display="block">\|\mathbf u + \mathbf v\| = \|\mathbf u\| + \|\mathbf v\|</math>  holds if and only if the triangle formed by {{math|'''u'''}}, {{math|'''v'''}}, and {{math|'''u''' + '''v'''}} is degenerate; that is, {{math|'''u'''}} and {{math|'''v'''}} are on the same ray, i.e., {{math|'''u''' {{=}} 0}} or {{math|'''v''' {{=}} 0}} or {{math|'''u''' {{=}} ''α''&hairsp;'''v'''}} for some {{math|''α'' > 0}}.<ref>{{Cite web| title=On the triangle equality - Grzegorz Łysik | url=https://files.ele-math.com/abstracts/mia-21-36-abs.pdf | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180721003127/http://files.ele-math.com/abstracts/mia-21-36-abs.pdf | archive-date=2018-07-21}}</ref> 

This property characterizes strictly convex normed spaces such as the {{mvar|ℓ<sub>p</sub>}} spaces with {{math|1 < ''p'' < ∞}}. However, there are normed spaces in which this is not true. For instance, consider the plane with the {{math|''ℓ''<sub>1</sub>}} norm (the [[Manhattan distance]]) and denote {{math|'''u''' {{=}} (1, 0)}} and {{math|'''v''' {{=}} (0, 1)}}. Then the triangle formed by {{math|'''u'''}}, {{math|'''v'''}}, and {{math|'''u''' + '''v'''}}, is non-degenerate but

<math display=block>\|\mathbf u+\mathbf v\|=\|(1,1)\|=|1|+|1|=2=\|\mathbf u\|+\|\mathbf v\|.</math>

===Example norms===
The ''[[absolute value]]'' is a norm for the [[real line]]; as required, the absolute value satisfies the triangle inequality for any real numbers {{mvar|u}} and {{mvar|v}}. 
*If {{mvar|u}} and {{mvar|v}} have the same sign or either of them is zero, then <math display=block>|u + v| = |u|+|v|.</math> 
*If {{mvar|u}} and {{mvar|v}} have opposite signs, then [[without loss of generality]] assume <math>|u| > |v|.</math> Then <math display=block>|u + v| = |u| - |v| < |u| + |v|.</math> 
Combining these cases:<ref name=Stewart>A proof not requiring separate cases is as follows: Any number is always less than or equal to its own absolute value, so <math>-|u| \leq u \leq |u|</math> and <math>-|v| \leq v \leq |v|.</math> Adding these inequalities together, <math>-\bigl(|u| + |v|\bigr) \leq u+v \leq |u| + |v|,</math> the sum has the form <math>-a \leq b \leq a</math> for <math>a = |u| + |v|</math> and <math>b = u + v.</math> But this always implies <math>| b | \leq a</math>, or, expanded, <math>|u + v| \leq |u|+|v|.</math> {{pb}} {{cite book |page=A10 |author=James Stewart |title=Essential Calculus |url=https://archive.org/details/studentsolutions0000stew |url-access=registration |isbn=978-0-495-10860-3 |publisher=Thomson Brooks/Cole |year=2008}}</ref>

<math display="block">|u + v| \leq |u|+|v|.</math>

The triangle inequality is useful in [[mathematical analysis]] for determining the best upper estimate on the size of the sum of two numbers, in terms of the sizes of the individual numbers. There is also a lower estimate, which can be found using the ''reverse triangle inequality'' which states that for any real numbers {{mvar|u}} and {{mvar|v}}, 
<math display=block>|u-v| \geq \bigl||u|-|v|\bigr|.</math>The ''[[Absolute value|modulus]]'' of a complex number is a generalization of the absolute value to the complex plane and is a norm for the complex numbers, regarded as a one-dimensional complex vector space or as a two-dimensional real vector space.  For a complex number <math>z=x+iy,\ (x,y\in\mathbb{R}), </math> it is defined by <math>|z|=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}.</math>  For a complex number expressed in polar form, <math>z=re^{i\theta},</math> with <math>r\geq 0</math> and <math>\theta\in[0,2\pi),</math> it is given by <math>|z|=r.</math>  For complex numbers <math>u,v\in\mathbb{C},</math> the triangle inequality holds.  The triangle inequality follows from the observation that there exists <math>c\in\mathbb{C}</math> such that <math>|c|=1</math> and <math>c(u+v)=|u+v|.</math><ref>If <math>w=u+v=re^{i\theta}</math> is nonzero, let <math>c=e^{-i\theta}.</math>  If <math>w=0,</math> simply let <math>c=1.</math></ref>  From this, the following computation gives the triangle inequality:

<math display="block">|u+v|=c(u+v)=cu+cv=\mathrm{Re}(cu)+\mathrm{Re}(cv) \leq |cu|+|cv|=|u|+|v|.</math>

The third equality in the chain follows from the fact that <math>cu+cv</math> is real, while the inequality in the chain follows from the fact that for any complex number <math>z=x+iy</math> written in rectangular form, <math>\mathrm{Re}(z)=x\leq\sqrt{x^2+y^2}=|z|.</math>

The ''[[taxicab norm]]'' or 1-norm is one generalization absolute value to higher dimensions. To find the norm of a vector <math>v = (v_1, v_2, \ldots v_n ),</math> just add the absolute value of each component separately, <math display="block">\|v\|_1 = |v_1| + |v_2| + \dotsb + |v_n|.</math>

The ''Euclidean norm'' or 2-norm defines the length of translation vectors in an {{mvar|n}}-dimensional [[Euclidean space]] in terms of a [[Cartesian coordinate system]]. For a vector <math>v = (v_1, v_2, \ldots v_n ),</math> its length is defined using the {{mvar|n}}-dimensional [[Pythagorean theorem]]: 
<math display="block">\|v\|_2 = \sqrt{|v_1|^2 + |v_2|^2 + \dotsb + |v_n|^2}.</math>

The ''inner product'' is norm in any [[inner product space]], a generalization of Euclidean vector spaces including infinite-dimensional examples. The triangle inequality follows from the [[Cauchy–Schwarz inequality]] as follows: Given vectors {{mvar|u}} and {{mvar|v}}, and denoting the inner product as <math>\langle u , v\rangle</math>:<ref name="Stillwell">{{cite book |title=The four pillars of geometry |author=John Stillwell |page=[https://archive.org/details/fourpillarsofgeo0000stil/page/80 80] |url=https://archive.org/details/fourpillarsofgeo0000stil |url-access=registration |isbn=0-387-25530-3 |year=2005 |publisher=Springer}}</ref>

<math display="block">\begin{align}
  \|u + v\|^2 &= \langle u + v, u + v \rangle \\
  &= \|u\|^2 + \langle u, v \rangle + \langle v, u \rangle + \|v\|^2 \\
  &\le \|u\|^2 + 2|\langle u, v \rangle| + \|v\|^2 \\
  &\le \|u\|^2 + 2\|u\|\|v\| + \|v\|^2 \quad \text{(by Cauchy–Schwarz inequality)} \\
  &=  \left(\|u\| + \|v\|\right)^2
\end{align}</math>

The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality turns into an equality if and only if {{mvar|u}} and {{mvar|v}} are linearly dependent. The inequality <math>\langle u, v \rangle + \langle v, u \rangle \le 2\left|\left\langle u, v \right\rangle\right|</math> turns into an equality for linearly dependent {{mvar|u}} and  {{mvar|v}} if and only if one of the vectors {{mvar|u}} or {{mvar|v}} is a ''nonnegative'' scalar of the other. Taking the square root of the final result gives the triangle inequality.

The [[p-norm|{{mvar|p}}-norm]] is a generalization of taxicab and Euclidean norms, using an arbitrary positive integer exponent, 
<math display="block">\|v\|_p = \bigl(|v_1|^p + |v_2|^p + \dotsb + |v_n|^p\bigr)^{1/p},</math> 
where the {{mvar|v<sub>i</sub>}} are the components of vector {{mvar|v}}.

Except for the case {{math|1=''p'' = 2}}, the {{mvar|p}}-norm is ''not'' an inner product norm, because it does not satisfy the [[parallelogram law]]. The triangle inequality for general values of {{mvar|p}} is called [[Minkowski's inequality]].<ref name="Saxe">{{cite book |title=Beginning functional analysis |author= Karen Saxe|author-link= Karen Saxe |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=0LeWJ74j8GQC&pg=PA61 |page=61 |isbn=0-387-95224-1 |publisher=Springer |year=2002}}</ref> It takes the form:
<math display="block">\|u+v\|_p \le \|u\|_p + \|v\|_p \ .</math>

==Metric space==
In a [[metric space]] {{mvar|M}} with metric {{mvar|d}}, the triangle inequality is a requirement upon [[Metric (mathematics)#Definition|distance]]:
<math display=block>d(A,\ C) \le d(A,\ B) + d(B,\ C) \ ,</math>

for all points {{mvar|A}}, {{mvar|B}}, and {{mvar|C}} in {{mvar|M}}. That is, the distance from {{mvar|A}} to {{mvar|C}} is at most as large as the sum of the distance from {{mvar|A}} to {{mvar|B}} and the distance from {{mvar|B}} to {{mvar|C}}.

The triangle inequality is responsible for most of the interesting structure on a metric space, namely, convergence.  This is because the remaining requirements for a metric are rather simplistic in comparison.  For example, the fact that any [[limit of a sequence|convergent sequence]] in a metric space is a [[Cauchy sequence]] is a direct consequence of the triangle inequality, because if we choose any {{mvar|x<sub>n</sub>}} and {{mvar|x<sub>m</sub>}} such that 
<math display=block>
  d(x_n, x) < \frac{\varepsilon}{2}, \quad 
d(x_m, x) < \frac{\varepsilon}{2},</math>
where {{math|''ε'' > 0}} is given and arbitrary (as in the definition of a limit in a metric space), then by the triangle inequality, 

<math display=block>d(x_n, x_m) \leq d(x_n, x) + d(x_m, x) < \frac{\varepsilon}{2} + \frac{\varepsilon}{2} = \varepsilon,</math>

so that the sequence {{math|{{mset|''x<sub>n</sub>''}}}} is a Cauchy sequence, by definition.

This version of the triangle inequality reduces to the one stated above in case of normed vector spaces where a metric is induced via 
<math display=block>d(u, v) := \| u-v \|,</math>
with {{math|''u'' − ''v''}} being the vector pointing from point {{mvar|v}} to {{mvar|u}}.

==Reverse triangle inequality==
The '''reverse triangle inequality''' is an equivalent alternative formulation of the triangle inequality that gives lower bounds instead of upper bounds. For plane geometry, the statement is:<ref name=inequality>
{{cite book |title=The popular educator; fourth volume |chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=lTACAAAAQAAJ&pg=PA196 |page=196 |chapter=Exercise I. to proposition XIX |year=1854 |publisher=John Cassell |location=Ludgate Hill, London |author=Anonymous}}
</ref>

:''Any side of a triangle is greater than or equal to the difference between the other two sides''.

In the case of a normed vector space, the statement is:
<math display=block>\big|\|u\|-\|v\|\big| \leq \|u-v\|,</math>
or, for metric spaces:
<math display=block>|d(A, C) - d(B, C)| \leq d(A, B).</math>
This implies that the norm <math>\|\cdot\|</math> as well as the distance-from-{{mvar|z}} function {{math|''d''(''z'', &centerdot;)}} are [[Lipschitz continuity|Lipschitz continuous]] with Lipschitz constant {{math|1}}, and therefore are in particular [[uniform continuity|uniformly continuous]].

The proof of the reverse triangle inequality from the usual one uses 
<math display=block>\begin{align} 
  \|v-u\| &= \|{-}1(u-v)\| \\[2pt]
  &= |{-}1|\cdot\|u-v\| \\[2pt]
  &= \|u-v\| 
\end{align}</math> 
to find:
<math display=block>\begin{align}
  \|u\| = \|(u-v) + v\| &\leq \|u-v\| + \|v\| \\[4pt]
  \Rightarrow \quad \|u\| - \|v\| &\leq \|u-v\|, \\[10pt]
  \|v\| = \|(v-u) + u\| &\leq \|v-u\| + \|u\| \\[4pt]
  \Rightarrow \quad \|u\| - \|v\| &\geq -\|u-v\|,
\end{align}</math>

Combining these two statements gives:
<math display=block>\begin{align}
  &-\|u-v\| \leq \|u\|-\|v\| \leq \|u-v\|  \\[4pt]
  &\Rightarrow \quad \big|\|u\|-\|v\|\big| \leq \|u-v\|.
\end{align}</math>

In the converse, the proof of the triangle inequality from the reverse triangle inequality works in two cases:

*If <math>\|u +v\| - \|u\| \geq 0,</math> then by the reverse triangle inequality,<math display=block>
\begin{align}
  &\|u +v\| - \|u\| = {\big|}\|u + v\|-\|u\|{\big|} \leq \|(u + v) - u\| = \|v\|  \\[4pt]
  &\Rightarrow \quad \|u + v\| \leq \|u\| + \|v\|
\end{align}
</math>
*And if <math>\|u +v\| - \|u\| < 0,</math> then trivially <math display=block>
  \|u\| +\|v\| \geq \|u\| > \|u + v\|
</math> by the nonnegativity of the norm. 

Thus, in both cases, we find that 
<math display=block>\|u\| + \|v\| \geq \|u + v\|.</math>

For metric spaces, the proof of the reverse triangle inequality is found similarly by:
<math display=block>\begin{align}
  d(A, B) + d(B, C) &\geq d(A, C) \\[4pt]
  \Rightarrow \quad d(A, B) &\geq d(A, C) - d(B, C) \\[10pt]
  d(C, A) + d(A, B) &\geq d(C, B) \\[4pt]
  \Rightarrow \quad d(A, B) &\geq d(B, C) - d(A, C)
\end{align}</math>
Putting these equations together we find:
<math display=block>d(A, B) \geq |d(A, C) - d(B, C)|</math>

And in the converse, beginning from the reverse triangle inequality, we can again use two cases:

*If <math>d(A, C) - d(B, C) \geq 0</math>, then <math display=block>
\begin{align}
  &d(A, B) \geq |d(A, C) - d(B, C)| = d(A, C) - d(B, C) \\[4pt]
  &\Rightarrow \quad d(A, B) + d(B, C) \geq d(A, C)
\end{align}</math>
*And if <math>d(A, C) - d(B, C) < 0,</math> then <math display=block>
  d(A, B) + d(B, C) \geq d(B, C) > d(A, C)
</math> again by the nonnegativity of the metric. 

Thus, in both cases, we find that 
<math display=block>d(A, B) + d(B, C) \geq d(A, C).</math>

==Reversal in Minkowski space==

The [[Minkowski space]] metric <math>\eta_{\mu \nu}</math> is not positive-definite, which means that <math>\|u\|^2 = \eta_{\mu \nu} u^\mu u^\nu</math> can have either sign or vanish, even if the vector {{mvar|u}} is non-zero. Moreover, if {{mvar|u}} and {{mvar|v}} are both timelike vectors lying in the future [[light cone]], the triangle inequality is reversed:

<math display="block">\|u+v\| \geq \|u\| + \|v\|.</math>

A physical example of this inequality is the [[twin paradox]] in [[special relativity]]. The same reversed form of the inequality holds if both vectors lie in the past light cone, and if one or both are null vectors. The result holds in <math>n + 1</math> dimensions for any <math>n \geq 1</math>.  If the plane defined by <math>u</math> and <math>v</math> is space-like (and therefore a Euclidean subspace) then the usual triangle inequality holds.
